newsitem.title: USA: Air Force adultery case sparks major debate.
newsitem.headline: Air Force adultery case sparks major debate.

text.p: The U.S. military's latest sex case, pitting the Air Force against its first woman bomber pilot, has fuelled an emotional debate over the military's strict rules and whether men and women get equal treatment.

The now-delayed adultery trial of B-52 pilot Lt. Kelly Flinn is inundating television and has even made strange bedfellows of the liberal New York Times and powerful conservative Republican Sen. Trent Lott of Mississippi.

Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall is deciding whether to allow Flinn to resign honourably or to proceed with a court martial at Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota, on charges of having an affair with a married man, having sex with a single enlisted man, disobeying an order and lying.
The military says adultery, "fraternizing" (socializing) with personnel of lower rank and the other charges are criminal acts and should be firmly punished.
Citing statistics, it says men in uniform get the same treatment in such cases.

But critics -- including Lott, the Times, the National Organisation for Women (NOW) and several members of Congress -- say the Air Force has bungled the case badly against the 26-year-old unmarried officer and should back off.

"Kelly Flinn is not innocent -- but neither is the Air Force. This case has been bungled from the very beginning," said New York Democratic Representative Nita Lowey at a news conference by several congresswomen angry at the case.
"The Air Force should have offered Kelly Flinn counselling, warnings, and a transfer. Instead it has thrown the book at her, treating her like a criminal," she said.

As with the Navy's 1991 "Tailhook" sex harassment scandal and the Army's recent problems over rape of female recruits by male drill sergeants, the Flinn case has raised questions about equal treatment of male and female troops.
The case sparked an angry exchange during a Senate committee hearing when Iowa Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin said: "I think the Air Force is looking ridiculous on this."
Gen. Ronald Fogleman, the Air Force chief of staff who was answering questions about his service's budget, retorted: "It makes us look ridiculous because people don't know the facts."
He asserted the issue was not one of adultery, but of an officer entrusted to fly planes carrying nuclear weapons who had mislead superiors and disobeyed orders.
"It's obvious that the Air Force and Flinn have painted each other into a corner here that neither can get out of gracefully," said retired Army Lt. Gen. James "Terry" Scott.

"The military says it treats men and women equally. I suspect that's true in this case, but some see it very differently," said Scott, a military analyst with Harvard's John F. Kennedy School of Government.
Air Force officials say it boils down to broader violations of the military code of conduct, including disobeying an order and lying during an investigation.
But Flinn's lawyers argue she is being unfairly persecuted for something commonplace in civilian life.
NOW spokeswoman Karen Johnson agreed. "She is being treated differently, singled out for more punishment than men who commit the same crime," she said.

"There were 140 male Navy and Marine officers accused of abusing 90 women at the the Tailhook meeting (in Las Vegas). Not one of those men, including the ones who lied about it, were court martialed," added Johnson, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel.
She also said a married male Air Force lieutenant colonel had an affair with his secretary at Minot last year and was not tried, but given a letter of reprimand and a fine.

Flinn, a St. Louis native and a 1993 graduate of the elite Air Force Academy in Colorado, has broken into tears in television interviews, saying the case has ruined her reputation as an icon for women in the armed services.

She became a bomber pilot in 1995 as the service began allowing women to fly warplanes, and is now one of only a few women qualified to fly big bombers such as the eight-engine B-52 and the swing-wing B-1.

Frank Spinner, Flinn's attorney, told reporters at Minot on Wednesday that the defence team had "received hundreds of letters about cases in which prosecutions have not taken place in similar situation."
"The Air Force is talking about consistency and equal justice under law and that's what we are asking for," he said.

The Army, Air Force and Navy are resisting efforts by some critics to force them to conduct separate training for men and women in the wake of charges that Army male drill sergeants have harassed and even raped female recruits.
But the Pentagon also recently ordered a study of fraternisation rules to make sure that they were being applied equally and were consistent across the services.
